title: Is there any point learning K-maps past 4 variables?
author: off_by_one
body:
Genuine question, not trying to start anything. Five and six variable maps exist but they're two or four stacked grids and you have to spot groupings *across* the layers. At that point I can't see the adjacency any more, which was the entire selling point.

So is the honest answer "use K-maps up to 4, use Quine-McCluskey or a tool past that"? Or is there a reason to push through?

replies.author: nandhole
replies.body:
honest answer: yes, 4 is the practical ceiling for doing it by eye, and that's fine.

the reason to learn K-maps at all isn't that you'll minimise real circuits with them, it's that they make *why* minimisation works visual. adjacent cells differ by one bit, so a group of 2^k adjacent cells means k variables don't matter and drop out. once that's in your head you understand what the algorithm is doing.

Quine-McCluskey is the same idea made mechanical, and it's exponential in the worst case anyway. real tools use Espresso, which is heuristic and doesn't guarantee a minimum.

replies.author: carry_the_one
replies.body:
Also nobody does two-level minimisation on real designs any more. You write behavioural HDL and the synthesiser does multi-level optimisation against an actual gate library with real timing and area costs. Minimum literal count isn't even the right objective.

Still worth understanding. Just don't expect to use it.

replies.author: heap_of_trouble
replies.body:
> don't-care conditions

The thing I'd add: the one place K-maps stay genuinely useful past coursework is reasoning about don't-cares. Being able to see that you can pick X = 1 here and get a much bigger group is a lot harder to feel from a truth table.
